patients.summary: Administrative assistant with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and SSc-associated PAH who joins in 2020, develops hypertension that becomes refractory and is found to be a pheochromocytoma with cortisol excess, then has nickel contact dermatitis, a hysterectomy complicated by ureteral injury, PAH progression, scleroderma renal crisis and, after her last visit, septic shock.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
34 y/o woman establishing care. Her last primary care office was out of the area and she wants someone closer to home and work (admin assistant).

PMH:
- Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis, dx 2018 by an outside rheumatology group, which she still sees once a year. Skin tightness of hands/forearms and trunk, stable per her.
- Pulmonary arterial hypertension, felt to be SSc-related, diagnosed 2019 at an outside PH clinic. On sildenafil 20 mg TID. Followed by PH cardiology yearly. Walks without trouble on flat ground.
- Heartburn, takes omeprazole 20 daily, controlled.
PSH: none.
Meds: sildenafil 20 mg TID, omeprazole 20 mg daily.
Allergies: nickel - itchy rash under cheap earrings and belt buckles. No drug allergies.
FHx: mother has lupus. Father has high blood pressure. No known adrenal tumors, endocrine tumor syndromes or neurofibromatosis in the family.
SHx: never smoker, no alcohol, no drugs. Lives in Amherst. Works full time at a desk.

ROS: no chest pain, no syncope, no edema, no dysphagia beyond occasional heartburn. Periods regular.

Exam: BP and vitals as recorded, normal today. Well appearing. Skin: thickened, shiny skin over fingers and dorsal hands, forearms; no ulcers. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abd soft, nontender. No edema.

A/P
1. Diffuse SSc - stable, rheum following. Will get their letters.
2. PAH on sildenafil - PH clinic following. Records request sent.
3. Health maintenance: Tdap today. HIV and hep C screening once, she agrees. Labs: CBC, CMP, UA, lipids. Pap was 2019 at her old office, records requested. PHQ-2 negative.
RTC 6 months or with the physical next fall.

documents.title: Your recent lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Susan, all of your labs from Monday look good. Kidney function, blood counts, liver tests and cholesterol are in the normal range, and your urine showed no protein or blood. HIV and hepatitis C screens were negative. Nothing to change. Nice to meet you.

Outside rheumatology group
Date of visit: 2021-03-22

Dear colleague,
I saw Ms. Jean-Baptiste for her yearly review of diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis. She feels well. Skin thickening over the hands, forearms and anterior chest is unchanged from last year by my exam. No digital ulcers. No new joint, muscle or bowel complaints. Current medications: sildenafil 20 mg three times daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily. Allergy: nickel.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Home readings have jumped since about New Year's - many in the 150s-160s over upper 90s despite amlodipine 10, lisinopril 20 and HCTZ 25, which she takes every day (pill box, pharmacy fill dates on time). For about a month she has also had spells: heart suddenly pounding, drenched in sweat, and a hard, pounding headache. They come out of nowhere, at her desk or at home, and last 10-20 minutes. Two or three a week. No chest pain, no syncope, no new meds, no decongestants, no caffeine change, no weight loss she knows of.

O: BP 158/98, recheck 156/96. HR regular. Not diaphoretic now. Thyroid not enlarged, no tremor. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. No edema.

A/P: BP now uncontrolled on three agents, with paroxysmal palpitations/sweats/headache. Thinking about a secondary cause. Today BMP and TSH. Asked her to write down each spell with time and a BP reading if she can grab one. If BMP and TSH are normal and this continues, I'd like endocrine to see her. Back in 6-8 weeks, sooner if a reading is over 180/110 or a spell includes chest pain or fainting.

documents.title: Endocrinology Consultation
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Outside endocrinology - new patient consultation
Date of service: 2023-07-24
Referred by: PCP, for resistant hypertension with spells

History: 37-year-old woman with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and SSc-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension. Over roughly six months her blood pressure has become difficult to control even though she reliably takes amlodipine, lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide. Alongside this she has unpredictable attacks of palpitations, heavy sweating and severe headache; some come with a feeling of impending doom.
Other history: SSc (2018), PAH on sildenafil (2019), heartburn. No surgeries.
Medications: amlodipine 10 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, sildenafil 20 mg three times daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily.
Allergies: nickel (contact dermatitis).
Family history: mother - SLE. Father - essential hypertension. No relatives known to have pheochromocytoma, neurofibromatosis or an MEN syndrome.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol. Administrative assistant.

Exam: BP 162/98, HR 102. Anxious-appearing. Abdomen: no palpable mass, no bruit.

Results (drawn today, random, seated):
- Plasma free metanephrine 1.2 nmol/L (reference < 0.5)
- Plasma free normetanephrine 2.4 nmol/L (reference < 0.9)

Impression: Catecholamine excess well above the range expected from interfering drugs or stress, with a classic paroxysmal history. Pheochromocytoma. Her hypertension is best regarded as severe and secondary to it.

Plan:
1. Start phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily. Liberal salt and fluids; expect stuffy nose and some orthostasis.
2. Once alpha blockade is established (2-3 weeks), we will add a beta blocker for heart rate. No beta blocker before then.
3. Continue amlodipine, lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide and sildenafil for now.
4. Return to endocrinology in 3 months.

Thank you for this referral.
Endocrinology

documents.title: Endocrinology Follow-up
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Outside endocrinology - return visit
Date of service: 2023-10-23

Interval: 37-year-old with diffuse SSc, SSc-PAH and pheochromocytoma, on phenoxybenzamine and atenolol since the summer. The adrenergic spells are much reduced. New concern: for about six months she has noticed her face getting rounder and fuller, her thighs and shoulders getting weaker (hard to climb stairs or lift files overhead), bruising with minimal bumps, more fatigue, and periods that have become irregular.
Medications: phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BID, atenolol 50 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, sildenafil 20 mg TID, omeprazole 20 mg daily.
Allergies: nickel (contact dermatitis).

Exam: BP 152/94. Scattered bruises on both upper arms. Proximal muscle weakness, hip flexors and deltoids 4/5.

Testing (arranged before this visit):
- Fasting glucose 112 mg/dL
- ACTH undetectable, < 5 pg/mL
- Serum cortisol 8 AM baseline 23.4 ug/dL; after high-dose overnight dexamethasone 22.9 ug/dL - no suppression

Impression: Cortisol excess that is ACTH-independent, with failure to suppress on high-dose dexamethasone. Given her catecholamine-secreting adrenal tumor, we attribute the cortisol excess to the same adrenal source.

Plan: continue phenoxybenzamine and atenolol. No new medication today. Return in 3 months. Glucose to be followed with her PCP.
Endocrinology

No new meds from them. Fasting glucose 112 there. She is tired, weaker on stairs. Spells rare now. Periods irregular since spring - some months heavier.

Meds: phenoxybenzamine 10 BID, atenolol 50, amlodipine 10, lisinopril 20, HCTZ 25, sildenafil 20 TID, omeprazole 20. Allergy nickel.

Exam: BP 138/86. Rounder face than last year. Bruises upper arms. Proximal strength mildly reduced. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abd soft, no mass. Skin thickening hands/forearms/chest as before. No edema.

A/P
1. Pheochromocytoma with cortisol excess - endocrinology following, next visit in 3 months.
2. Secondary HTN - better than spring. Continue.
3. Glucose - CMP today; endocrine asked us to follow.
4. Irregular menses - watch; tell me if bleeding gets heavy.
5. Prevention: flu + updated COVID today. PHQ-2 1. Pap due 2024.
Labs today.

documents.title: Dermatology Consultation
documents.author: dermatology
documents.body:
Outside dermatology
Date of visit: 2024-01-16
Reason for referral: wrist rash

This is a 37-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis, a pheochromocytoma and known nickel sensitivity. About three weeks ago an itchy rash appeared on her left wrist shortly after she began wearing a new wristwatch. She took the watch off three days ago but the rash has not settled. No change in laundry products or soap. She does dab perfume on both wrists most days. The area itches and burns. She feels otherwise well.

Medications: phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BID, atenolol 50 mg daily (since last summer), amlodipine 10 mg, lisinopril 20 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, sildenafil 20 mg TID, omeprazole 20 mg.
Allergies: nickel - contact dermatitis.

Exam: Eczematous, itchy plaque on the left wrist in the footprint of the watch back and band, with burning on palpation. No eruption elsewhere. No systemic signs.

Assessment: Allergic contact dermatitis of the left wrist from nickel in the watch. Fragrance applied to the same site is a probable additional contact allergen; we have added fragrance to her allergy list.

Plan:
1. Triamcinolone 0.1% cream to the wrist twice daily for two weeks, then stop.
2. Avoid nickel against the skin; a coat of clear nail polish on metal backs, or a nickel-free band.
3. Fragrance-free soaps, lotions and no perfume on the skin.
4. Return as needed.
Dermatology

We discussed medical options and surgery. She would like definitive treatment and chooses total abdominal hysterectomy. Risks reviewed, including bleeding, infection, and injury to bowel, bladder or ureters.
I spoke with her endocrinologist, who is comfortable with surgery on her current phenoxybenzamine and atenolol, and with her pulmonary hypertension cardiologist regarding anesthesia planning.
Plan: total abdominal hysterectomy, to be scheduled for July.

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
reports.text:
Indication: lower abdominal pain, postoperative day 1 after total abdominal hysterectomy.
Technique: axial images of the abdomen and pelvis after intravenous contrast.
Findings: Large volume of free fluid in the peritoneal cavity. No dilated or thickened bowel loops, no free intraperitoneal air beyond expected postoperative change, no bowel wall discontinuity. No organized or rim-enhancing collection. Postsurgical changes of hysterectomy at the vaginal cuff. Liver, spleen and pancreas unremarkable. Kidneys enhance symmetrically.
reports.conclusion: Large-volume peritoneal fluid after hysterectomy. No evidence of bowel injury or intra-abdominal abscess.

documents.title: Gynecology Discharge Summary
documents.author: gynecology
documents.body:
Area hospital - gynecology inpatient service
Admitted: 2024-07-16   Discharged: 2024-07-22
Procedure: total abdominal hysterectomy (2024-07-16) for menorrhagia
Allergies: nickel; fragrances

Hospital course:
Surgery on 7/16 was completed as planned. Phenoxybenzamine and atenolol were continued perioperatively at endocrinology's direction.
About twelve hours after surgery she developed constant lower abdominal pain that did not radiate. She had no nausea or vomiting and no change in bowel function. On POD 1 (7/17): BP 130/85, HR 90, T 37.2 C. Abdomen mildly distended and diffusely tender without rebound or guarding; no CVA tenderness. Urine output had been normal since the operation. Labs: hemoglobin 12.5, WBC 11.0, creatinine 0.9, BUN 14; urinalysis normal without blood or pyuria.
CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast showed a large amount of peritoneal fluid without bowel injury or abscess.
Given the volume of fluid, urology was consulted. Cystoscopy with left retrograde study on 7/18 showed contrast extravasation from the left distal ureter, consistent with an operative laceration. A left ureteral stent was placed. Pain improved over the following days, she tolerated diet, ambulated and voided normally around the stent. Pain controlled with oral analgesics in hospital.

Discharge diagnoses: s/p total abdominal hysterectomy for menorrhagia; iatrogenic left ureteral laceration, stented.
Discharge medications: unchanged home medications (phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BID, atenolol 50 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, sildenafil 20 mg TID, omeprazole 20 mg daily). [Hydrochlorothiazide not listed on our medication reconciliation.]
Follow-up: urology in about 6 weeks for stent removal; gynecology wound check 2 weeks; PCP within 1 week.
Gynecology

reports.text: PA and lateral views. Lungs clear without infiltrate, effusion or pneumothorax. Cardiomediastinal silhouette within normal limits. No structural abnormality of the bony thorax.

documents.title: Cardiology Follow-up Letter
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Cardiology - pulmonary hypertension program
Visit: 2025-01-20

Reason: scheduled follow-up of systemic sclerosis-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Over the past several months she has become steadily more short of breath with exertion - stairs and hills now wind her - and now and then has a dull chest discomfort while exerting. Her ankles are a little puffy by evening. She has no orthopnea, no paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea and no recent infections.
She also mentions that her fingers sometimes change color in the cold; she has never had this looked at.
Social: no tobacco, no recreational drugs.
Medications: sildenafil 20 mg TID, phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BID, atenolol 50 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, lisinopril 20 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, omeprazole 20 mg. Allergies: nickel, fragrances.

Exam: BP 126/78, HR 78, SpO2 97% - all within normal limits. Prominent, loud P2. Trace edema at both ankles. No rales or wheezes. No murmurs.

Studies today:
- Chest radiograph: no infiltrate or structural abnormality.
- Echocardiogram: enlarged right atrium and ventricle; LV size and function preserved.
- PFTs: unremarkable.
- ECG: right axis deviation, nonspecific ST-T changes.

Impression:
1. Progression of SSc-associated pulmonary arterial hypertension, now with right heart enlargement and exertional symptoms.
2. Cold-induced digital color change consistent with Raynaud phenomenon.

Plan: continue sildenafil 20 mg three times daily. Return in 6 months.
Cardiology

39-year-old with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and nickel contact allergy, seen by video for a left wrist rash that has recurred over three weeks, much like her January 2024 episode. documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Area hospital emergency department
Arrival: 2026-01-09 08:30

HPI: 39-year-old woman with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis, pulmonary arterial hypertension and a known pheochromocytoma. For two days she has had a severe headache with blurred vision and nausea. Vomiting has prevented her from keeping down any of her blood pressure medicines. Sent in by her PCP's office.
Medications (home): phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BID, atenolol 50 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, sildenafil 20 mg TID, omeprazole 20 mg daily.
Allergies: nickel, fragrances (contact dermatitis).
Family history: mother SLE; father essential hypertension; no family pheochromocytoma, NF or MEN.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol. Administrative assistant.

Triage vitals: BP 220/120, HR 88, RR 18.
Exam: uncomfortable. Diffusely thickened skin. Tender over the extensor aspects of the joints. Fundoscopy: flame-shaped hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots in both eyes. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Neuro nonfocal.

Labs:
- Creatinine 3.2 mg/dL (her baseline 0.9)
- BUN 45 mg/dL
- Hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL
- Platelets 90,000/mm3
- Urinalysis: SG 1.010, trace protein, no cells, no casts
- Peripheral smear: schistocytes seen

MDM: Hypertensive emergency with retinopathy, acute kidney injury and microangiopathic hemolysis in a patient with diffuse SSc - scleroderma renal crisis until proven otherwise. Pheochromocytoma considered; presentation and renal findings fit renal crisis.
ED course: IV antiemetic, captopril started, rheumatology and nephrology aware.
Disposition: admitted to medicine, step-down.
Impression: scleroderma renal crisis; acute kidney injury.
Emergency Medicine

documents.title: Medicine Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
Area hospital - medicine service
Admission 2026-01-09, discharge 2026-01-16
Principal diagnosis: scleroderma renal crisis
Secondary: acute kidney injury; microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia from the renal crisis
Other problems: diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis; SSc-associated PAH; pheochromocytoma; Raynaud phenomenon
Allergies: nickel; fragrances

Course: Admitted from the ED with BP 220/120, retinal hemorrhages and exudates, creatinine 3.2 from a baseline of 0.9, anemia, low platelets and schistocytes. Nephrology and rheumatology consulted. Captopril was started and titrated every few hours to effect; blood pressure came down over the following days without precipitous drops. Antiemetics allowed oral intake by day 2 and her phenoxybenzamine, atenolol and other home medications were resumed. Creatinine peaked early and then improved slowly. No dialysis was required. Headache and vision improved.
Discharge labs (1/16): creatinine 2.4, hemoglobin 9.0, platelets 128,000.

Discharge medications: lisinopril 20 mg daily resumed in place of inpatient captopril; phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BID; atenolol 50 mg daily; amlodipine 10 mg daily; hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; sildenafil 20 mg TID; omeprazole 20 mg daily.
Follow-up: PCP in 1-2 weeks with BMP and CBC; rheumatology and nephrology clinic follow-up to be arranged by those services. Daily home BP; return for headache, vision change, or BP over 160/100.
Hospital Medicine

documents.title: ICU Admission Note
documents.author: critical care
documents.body:
Area hospital - emergency department to intensive care unit
Date of admission: 2026-07-18 (Saturday)

HPI: 40-year-old woman with diffuse cutaneous scleroderma, SSc-associated PAH, pheochromocytoma and a scleroderma renal crisis in January. Began with burning on urination and left flank pain. Over the next 24 hours she became more and more lethargic and has passed no urine.
Home medications: phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BID, atenolol 50 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, sildenafil 20 mg TID, omeprazole 20 mg daily.
Allergies: nickel, fragrances (contact dermatitis).

Vitals on arrival: T 39 C, BP 80/40, HR 100, RR 22.
Exam: acutely ill. Extremities cool, capillary refill delayed. Skin: no rash, petechiae or wounds.
Labs: creatinine 4.6 mg/dL, BUN 62 mg/dL, lactate 5.4 mmol/L, WBC 19.6 with 89% neutrophils. Blood cultures drawn, pending.

Assessment: septic shock, presumed urinary source, with acute kidney injury and anuria.
Plan: IV fluid resuscitation; norepinephrine for MAP goal; empiric broad-spectrum IV antibiotics after cultures; hold all antihypertensives; ICU admission. Further management per ICU team.
Critical Care
